stimulus.text: The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September and October 1774. Fifty-six delegates came from every colony except Georgia. The Congress agreed to a Continental Association — a pledge of nonimportation, nonexportation, and nonconsumption of British goods — and created local Committees of Safety to enforce the agreements. It also petitioned King George III for repeal of the Coercive Acts, and set May 10, 1775, as the date for a Second Continental Congress.

stem: The Congress's decision to petition King George III for repeal of the Coercive Acts most directly shows that...

options.text: The delegates had already decided to declare independence
options.misconception: A petition to the king is the opposite of a declaration — the delegates were asking for redress within the empire, not breaking from it.

options.text: The delegates believed Parliament had no authority over the colonies
options.misconception: The petition asks the king to repeal Parliament's acts — the delegates still worked through the king, which assumes the imperial system, not its rejection.

options.text: The delegates had given up on nonimportation as a tactic
options.misconception: The Congress adopted nonimportation at the same meeting — the petition and the boycott went together, not one instead of the other.

options.text: Most delegates still sought reconciliation within the British Empire

rationales.D: The Congress petitioned the king and set a date to meet again — the moves of people seeking redress, not separation. In 1774 most delegates still wanted reconciliation, not independence.
rationales.A: Independence was not decided in 1774. A petition to the king is a plea for redress inside the empire.
rationales.B: The petition works through the king, not around him. It assumes the imperial system still functions.
rationales.C: Nonimportation was adopted at the same meeting. The petition and the boycott were two tools, not alternatives.
rationales.general:
1. Read what the Congress did last. It petitioned the king for repeal — asking the empire's head to fix the problem.
2. Ask what a petition assumes. That the king might listen, and that the colonies still belong in the empire.
3. Ask what it rules out. A break: you do not petition a king you have already rejected.
Remember: the last thing a body does often tells you its real aim — a petition is a plea, not a farewell.
